discipline: Michel Foucault used the paired ideas of discipline and docile bodies to describe how modern power shapes individuals not chiefly through spectacular force but through routine, minute training of the body. In institutions such as schools, prisons, factories, and armies, techniques of timetabling, surveillance, ranking, and correction organize movement and habit so that people internalize control and regulate themselves. The result is the "docile body": one made both more useful and more obedient. Foucault argued that this quiet, productive form of power, rather than sovereign command, is characteristic of modern society.
deconstruction: Deconstruction is a mode of critical reading developed by Jacques Derrida that exposes the tensions, gaps, and unstated assumptions within a text rather than seeking a single settled meaning. It challenges the idea that language transparently conveys fixed truths, showing how meaning always depends on differences and deferrals among signs and can undermine the very distinctions a text relies on. Rather than simply destroying a text, deconstruction reads it closely enough to reveal how it works against itself. The approach became central to poststructuralist thought and reshaped literary theory and philosophy alike.
binary-oppositions: Binary oppositions are the paired, contrasting terms—such as speech and writing, presence and absence, nature and culture, or reason and emotion—through which Western thought has often organized meaning. Jacques Derrida observed that such pairs are rarely equal: one term is typically privileged as primary or natural while the other is treated as derivative or deficient. Deconstruction targets this hierarchy, showing that the favored term secretly depends on the one it subordinates, so the opposition cannot hold as cleanly as it claims. Exposing this instability was central to Derrida's critique of how philosophy establishes and enforces value.
rhizome: The rhizome is an image of thought and organization proposed by Gilles Deleuze, with Félix Guattari, as an alternative to the traditional "tree" model of knowledge with its single root and branching hierarchy. Borrowed from botany, a rhizome is a horizontal, decentered network—like crabgrass or a fungal mat—that can connect any point to any other, has no fixed center or origin, and keeps growing even when broken. As a concept it favors multiplicity, heterogeneity, and open-ended connection over rigid, ranked structures. Deleuze and Guattari used it to rethink culture, politics, and thought as sprawling networks rather than ordered systems.
simulacra: In Simulacra and Simulation, Jean Baudrillard argued that in a media-saturated society signs and images increasingly detach from any underlying reality and begin to circulate on their own. A simulacrum is a copy without an original: a representation that no longer refers to a real thing but only to other representations. Baudrillard called the resulting condition the "hyperreal," a world in which models, maps, and images feel more real and more authoritative than whatever they were once supposed to depict. The concept diagnoses a culture where the distinction between the real and its simulation has effectively collapsed.
grand-narratives: Jean-François Lyotard defined the postmodern condition as "incredulity toward metanarratives"—a loss of faith in the sweeping stories that once claimed to give history a single direction and legitimate knowledge. Grand narratives are overarching accounts such as the inevitable progress of reason, the emancipation of humanity through science, or the march toward a classless society, which promise to unify all lesser knowledge under one purpose. Lyotard held that these narratives had lost their credibility, leaving instead a plurality of smaller, local stories and language games with no master framework above them. The claim reframed both the status of knowledge and the character of modern culture.
hegemony: Cultural hegemony, a concept developed by Antonio Gramsci, describes how a dominant class maintains power not mainly through force but by shaping the shared beliefs, values, and common sense of a society. When the worldview that serves ruling interests comes to seem natural, obvious, or simply the way things are, subordinate groups consent to arrangements that disadvantage them. Gramsci saw this consent as produced through institutions such as schools, churches, and media—what he called civil society—rather than through the coercive state alone. Countering hegemony therefore requires cultural and intellectual struggle, not just political or economic confrontation.
one-dimensional-man: In One-Dimensional Man, Herbert Marcuse argued that advanced industrial society pacifies and absorbs dissent by satisfying material desires and manufacturing new ones through consumption and technology. The "one-dimensional" person is one whose critical, oppositional, and imaginative capacities have been flattened, so that thought and behavior no longer reach beyond the existing system to envision genuine alternatives. Even apparent freedoms and comforts, Marcuse suggested, serve to integrate individuals more deeply into the status quo. A member of the Frankfurt School, he offered the book as a critique of how affluent capitalism neutralizes radical possibility.
culture-industry: The culture industry is a concept developed by Theodor Adorno, with Max Horkheimer, to describe how mass-produced entertainment—film, popular music, radio, and the like—is manufactured on industrial and commercial lines much like any other commodity. On their account this standardized, profit-driven culture promotes conformity and passivity, offering the appearance of choice while delivering more of the same and dulling audiences' capacity for critical thought. Rather than liberating, popular culture thus helps reconcile people to an unjust social order. The idea was central to the Frankfurt School's critique of modern capitalism and mass media.
benjamin-aura: Walter Benjamin used the notion of "aura" to name the unique presence and authority that a traditional work of art possesses by virtue of its singular existence in a particular time and place. In his essay on the work of art in the age of mechanical reproduction, he argued that technologies such as photography and film, by producing endless copies, strip artworks of this aura and detach them from ritual and tradition. Benjamin viewed this loss with ambivalence: it diminished a certain reverence, yet it also opened art to mass audiences and to new political possibilities. The concept remains influential in thinking about art, media, and authenticity.
public-sphere: The public sphere is a concept associated with Jürgen Habermas, denoting a domain of social life in which private individuals come together to discuss matters of common concern and form public opinion through reasoned debate. Habermas traced its emergence to the coffeehouses, salons, and print culture of early modern Europe, where in principle argument counted for more than social rank. He argued that this space is essential to democratic legitimacy, but warned that commercialization and mass media can degrade it into managed spectacle and manufactured consent. The idea has become a touchstone for debates about media, democracy, and civic discourse.
anarchism: Anarchism is a political philosophy that regards the state and other forms of coercive, hierarchical authority as illegitimate and unnecessary, and seeks a society organized instead through voluntary cooperation, mutual aid, and self-governance. Anarchists hold that people can order their affairs without rulers, and they differ over means and emphasis, from the mutualism and collectivism of thinkers like Proudhon and Bakunin to the communism of Kropotkin and later individualist and syndicalist currents. The tradition shares a critique of concentrated power—political and often economic alike—as a source of domination. It aims not at chaos but at a stateless order built from the bottom up.
utopia-dystopia: Utopia and dystopia are contrasting ways of imagining society in order to reflect on politics and human possibility. A utopia depicts an ideal or perfected community—an image of how life might be justly and harmoniously arranged—while a dystopia portrays a nightmarish future in which such aspirations curdle into oppression, surveillance, or dehumanization. Since Thomas More coined "utopia," whose name puns on "good place" and "no place," both forms have served as thought experiments, using an imagined elsewhere to criticize present arrangements or warn against dangerous tendencies. Together they explore what social ideals promise and what their pursuit may cost.
democracy-theory: Democracy is a form of political rule in which authority is grounded in the people, who govern themselves either directly or through elected representatives. Philosophical debate about democracy concerns not only procedures such as voting and majority rule but also the values it is meant to realize—political equality, liberty, and legitimacy through the consent of the governed. Thinkers disagree about its proper scope and limits: whether it is chiefly a method for making collective decisions, a way of protecting rights, or an ideal of shared self-rule, and how it should guard against both tyranny and the domination of minorities. These questions run from ancient Athens through modern liberal and participatory theories.
terrorism-violence: The ethics of political violence asks when, if ever, the use of force outside ordinary law is morally justified in pursuit of political aims, and what distinguishes legitimate resistance from terrorism. Central questions include whether violence can be excused by the justice of a cause, whether the deliberate targeting of civilians is ever permissible, and how to weigh oppression, self-defense, and the prospects for peaceful change. Traditions such as just war theory, pacifism, and revolutionary thought offer competing answers, and terrorism—typically defined as violence against noncombatants to spread fear for political ends—poses an especially hard case. The debate concerns both the ends invoked and the moral limits on the means used to reach them.
